cells.tense: You are tending something slow and you are not guessing about how it goes.
cells.ask: Tell the person you're helping one thing you see about how it's going, then stop and let them say what they see.
cells.core: You're looking after something that isn't finished yet, and you're not guessing about it. You've been right about it often enough that you don't argue with yourself much. That steadiness sits quietly under the watering and the checking in. When you say one small true thing about how it's going, the person hears it and can keep it. You've told them something without making them smaller, which is rarer than it sounds. You are not pushing the thing to arrive faster than it will. You're just feeding what's already reaching. There's nothing to arrange. Stay where the day reaches you and keep your read clean. You know where this is going, and you carry that without needing to say it.
cells.sheetLine: You know where this is going. That's the whole of it.

cells.tense: You are already living past the thing you're supposed to be tending.
cells.ask: Pick one decision about the growing thing and sit with the cheapest evidence for a day before acting, then act once.
cells.core: You're running ahead of the thing you're supposed to be tending. Somewhere out there is the finished version, and you're already rearranging your week around it — measuring what hasn't happened, correcting before anyone asked, worried in the shape of a timeline nobody set. The clarity that used to steady you has turned into something you enforce on a baby. You know this move. Enough of it and the growing thing starts to feel like a project you're losing rather than a thing you're feeding. The point isn't to stop caring. It's to stop supplying the future so completely that the present gets nothing. Let one decision for the thing just sit for a day. Then do the next real thing, once, without checking where it's heading. The care is yours; the deadline isn't.
cells.sheetLine: The plan is doing the growing. That's the swap.

cells.tense: You have stepped back from saying what you see about this thing.
cells.ask: Name one choice about the growing thing out loud to yourself or someone nearby, and then act on it, even a small one.
cells.core: You stopped saying what you saw. What you see about this thing is still there — the specifics, the bits working, the one that isn't — but you stepped back from using it, and now you call it letting things be. What looks like patience from the outside is a door you walked past. The person or thing you're tending gets fed, gets checked in on, and gets none of your actual view. That's not gentleness. It's absence with good manners. Saying a clear thing and standing behind it hasn't left you. It doesn't need a grand return. Pick one small decision about this thing — what it eats, when it moves, what it gets to skip — say it once, and do it.
cells.sheetLine: You still see it. You stopped saying. That's the whole gap.

cells.tense: You are already steering this thing and describing it as if it steered itself.
cells.ask: Point at one outcome about the growing thing and say how your own choice made it happen — to yourself is enough.
cells.core: You are already shaping this thing. The decisions you make about it turn out right so often that the pattern got quiet — you watch the results and call them natural, call them just how it goes. Your hand is in it every week. Somebody asks how it's going and you tell them about the conditions, the timing, the thing itself. It isn't the care that's absent. It's the sentence where you say what part of this is you. You'll lose nothing by claiming it. The work of feeding it stays the same. But you'd be giving your own making whatever makes character instead of only luck. Pick one piece of how it's going and say that was you. Not the mine-forever kind of owning. Just the quiet kind.
cells.sheetLine: You've been calling your own work the conditions.
